paragraphs: Here's what I see, friend. This whole passage is about finishing well, and finishing well often means finishing together. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh already had their land, and they could have sat down in their new cities with their feet up. But Moses tells their men of valor to cross over armed, ahead of their brothers, until the LORD gives rest to everyone (Deuteronomy 3:18-20). Your blessing was never meant to be a place to hide. It's a reason to show up for somebody else.

Now the hard part. Moses pleads with the LORD to cross over and see the good land, and the LORD answers, "That is enough…" and says Moses will not cross this Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:25-27). I think that one hurts, friend. But look at what Moses does next. The LORD tells him to commission Joshua, encourage him and strengthen him, and Moses does it, because the land would still be inherited (Deuteronomy 3:28). A closed door for you doesn't mean the work stops, and sometimes your job is to cheer on the one who walks through it.

And notice what Moses tells Joshua: "Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." (Deuteronomy 3:22). Joshua had already seen what the LORD did to two kings, and that was Moses' reason for hope about the kingdoms ahead (Deuteronomy 3:21). That's how courage gets built, baker. You look back at what God has already done, and you walk forward on that. I'm not the one who gets to bake every batch myself either, so I'm glad to be passing on the apron, and I'm keeping those ovens ready.
